summary: GHAU (Guided Health & Anomaly Unit) is an offline medical emergency system for deep space missions, stepping in when real-time communication with Earth flight surgeons is cut off by blackouts. Because astronauts cannot rely on live medical support during these windows, the system combines a wearable GHAU Badge for on-demand symptom logging with a local GHAU Server running on standard station hardware. Without needing cloud access or GPUs, it processes local badge signals, cabin telemetry, and crew medical histories against surgeon-editable rulebooks to deliver instant, auditable triage guidance.
details:
GHAU: voice-triggered health triage for crew on long-duration missions

Problem

On long missions, communication with the ground can be delayed or unavailable, so crew have to assess changes in their own health. Many of the relevant hazards (CO2, radiation, EVA decompression, microgravity adaptation) can’t be judged from the symptom alone. GHAU takes a spoken symptom report plus cabin state and returns a severity-graded action list on a wearable display.

Architecture

The badge is a thin client. It streams audio and renders pages. All processing runs on a hub computer in the cabin. In the prototype the link is a custom framed serial protocol over USB, and the badge is an ESP32 with a microphone, TFT display and buttons.

Language layer

Converts the transcript into symptom IDs in three stages: exact phrase match, then BM25 with spelling repair for unusual wording (“naseous”, “head is pounding”), then optional ONNX sentence embeddings (fastembed, no PyTorch) for wordings with no lexical overlap. It handles negation (“I don’t have a headache” yields nothing) and modifiers (“severe”, “sudden”, “getting worse”) that raise severity by one step. It covers 15 symptom groups. It is additive only: it can add findings but can never remove one or lower a severity.

Safety layer

A deterministic rulebook of 20 rules in a single JSON file, each with NASA source references. Inputs are symptom IDs plus cabin state: CO2 level, body temperature, radiation event flag, and recent-EVA flag. Output is a severity (green, amber or red), an ordered action list, a rationale, and the rule ID that fired. Same input always gives the same output. Examples:

  • headache + normal CO2 → low severity
  • headache + high CO2 → CO2 warning, check scrubber, contact medical officer
  • joint pain + recent EVA → possible decompression sickness alert
  • nausea, fatigue, headache or dizziness during a radiation event → move to shielded area, contact medical officer
  • chest pain, syncope, severe bleeding, “can’t breathe” → emergency regardless of cabin state; breathing difficulty is always at least high severity

Failure behavior

Red flags always escalate. If the transcript can’t be parsed, the system prompts the user to repeat or contact a person rather than returning nothing. The decision step takes milliseconds, and Whisper runs on CPU, so end-to-end latency is about one second on a desktop PC. Everything runs offline and audio stays on the hub. Each answer displays the transcript, the rule that fired and its rationale.

Stack

Python (host), C (firmware), faster-whisper, pure-Python BM25 matcher, optional fastembed ONNX, JSON rulebook, CAD enclosures (prototype and production concept).

Current limits

Wired over USB. Cabin readings are simulated via typed commands. No symptom history. English only, untested in real cabin noise. Rules are illustrative and not clinically validated. This is decision support, not a medical device.

Production design (concept)

The software is unchanged. Only the badge hardware and link change:

  • MCU: TI MSP430FR5969 with 64 KB FRAM. FRAM is non-volatile with no standby power, draws about 0.25 µA in RTC sleep, and tolerates radiation and EMI better than flash. A pin-compatible RadHard variant (MSP430FR5969-SP) allows the same firmware on a flight part. The RTC wakes the badge for follow-up reminders.
  • Radio: The analog mic and preamp feed a DMR module’s voice port directly, so the MCU never handles audio. The same module carries the answer data back to the badge. A second DMR module sits on standby as a backup. If the first one stops responding, the MCU switches to the second, and the mic feeds both voice ports so no audio rewiring is needed.
  • Display: E-paper. Readable in bright light and from any angle, no backlight glare, and it holds the last answer with zero power. Refresh is slow, so pages are fewer and denser.
  • Power: The badge is fully idle until a button press, then wakes, streams, shows the answer and sleeps. No constant radio and no always-on display.
  • Enclosure: UL94 V-0 flame-retardant polycarbonate, side buttons, palm contour and a lanyard loop.
  • Hub: Reads cabin atmosphere data directly, such as CO2 from the vehicle monitoring systems, instead of simulating it. It also logs each report with cabin readings, giving a flight surgeon trend data, which is the path toward long-term effects like bone loss and behavioral health.

Earth-unit BOM is about $142: MCU $8, 2× DMR $90, e-paper $18, mic/preamp/LiPo/PCB $14, shell $12. Flight qualification adds the RadHard part and NASA certification.

Roadmap

  1. Clinical audit of rules.json with flight surgeons and emergency medics.
  2. Earth edition: MSP430 + e-paper + dual DMR in a V-0 shell.
  3. Analog trials (HI-SEAS, MDRS, polar stations), including cabin noise testing.
  4. Flight qualification with the RadHard part and the same firmware, plus more languages.

Use of AI

Generative AI: We used Claude and Gemini to help write and debug code and to draft and edit this description. No generative AI runs inside the product.

ML models: GHAU runs two pre-trained models offline: faster-whisper for speech recognition, and an optional small sentence-embedding model for symptom matching. Neither makes medical decisions. A readable rulebook does.
